messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
Is the forward direction the natural one? Let $(F_n)$ be a nested sequence of nonempty closed sets with $\operatorname{diam} F_n \to 0$, and pick $x_n \in F_n$. Is $(x_n)$ Cauchy? For $m > n$, both $x_m$ and $x_n$ lie in $F_n$, so $d(x_m, x_n) \le \operatorname{diam} F_n \to 0$. Completeness gives $x_n \to x \in M$. The tail $(x_k)_{k \ge n}$ lies in the closed set $F_n$ for each $n$, forcing $x \in F_n$, and hence $x \in \bigcap_n F_n$.

For the converse, suppose the intersection property holds. Must $M$ be complete? Let $(x_n)$ be a Cauchy sequence and define $F_n = \operatorname{cl}(\{x_k : k \ge n\})$. The sets $F_n$ are nonempty, closed, nested, and satisfy $\operatorname{diam} F_n \to 0$. Does the property apply? The property yields $x \in \bigcap_n F_n$. Does $x_n$ converge to $x$? Fix $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $N$ with $d(x_i, x_j) < \varepsilon/2$ for all $i, j \ge N$, and pick $k \ge N$ with $d(x_k, x) < \varepsilon/2$. Then $d(x_m, x) < \varepsilon$ for all $m \ge N$, confirming $M$ is complete. $\square$
